newsitem.title: USA: Congress has tough habit to kick -- tobacco money.
newsitem.headline: Congress has tough habit to kick -- tobacco money.

text.p: Congress has a tough habit to kick as it considers the landmark tobacco settlement -- the millions of dollars that candidates have received in campaign contributions from tobacco interests.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich was among the top 10 members of Congress in contributions received from the tobacco industry during the last election cycle. And Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the world's largest cigarette maker, contributed more so-called "soft" money to political campaigns than any other American corporation, watchdog groups said.
The tobacco industry and most states reached an agreement on Friday for tobacco companies to pay $368.5 billion in return for some protections from mounting lawsuits on behalf of smokers.

But the agreement must win the approval of Congress and the White House for it to become law, shifting new focus on the nearly three-out-of-four members of Congress who accept campaign contributions from the tobacco industry.

"Congress has to approve whatever agreement, and given the influence of tobacco on elected officials, the American public has to ask if that agreement is best for the American people," said Celia Wexler, a lobbyist for Common Cause, a public interest group that focuses on campaign spending issues.
Candidates ignore tobacco interests at their peril, given the high cost of running for office these days, Wexler said in an interview.
According to a survey by Common Cause, which is critical of the tobacco industry, 314 of the 435 current House members and 78 of the 100 senators have accepted tobacco money over the past 10 years.
The most influential members of Congress are among the top beneficiaries of tobacco largesse at campaign time.
Gingrich, a Republican from Georgia, took in $30,500 in tobacco money during the 1995-96 period, ranking seventh in the House in that time, according to the Centre for Responsive Politics.

House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, a Democrat from Missouri and possible presidential candidate, ranked fourth in the House from 1987 to 1996 by raking in $81,248. But contributions declined in recent years and Gephardt has stopped taking tobacco money.

The undisputed king of the tobacco sweepstakes is Sen. Jesse Helms, a Republican from the tobacco-growing state of North Carolina and a champion for the industry, who took in $52,250 in 1995-96 and $98,750 over the 10-year period.
The watchdog groups receive their information from the Federal Elections Commission, which is responsible for monitoring campaign financing and spending.

Tobacco industry campaign contributions totalled nearly $10 million in 1995-96. That included $2.8 million doled out by the industry's political action committees and some $300,000 from individual executives of tobacco firms.

As an industry, however, tobacco is well down the list in financing America's expensive political campaigns. According to Citizen Action, the banking, securities and finance sector is tops, dishing out $63.5 million to politicians in 1996 alone.
"It (tobacco) certainly doesn't compare to finance," Sheila Krumholz of the Centre for Responsive Politics said. "But it's a tiny industry. There are only a few heavy hitters."

However, where tobacco is really king is in the so-called soft money -- contributions largely unregulated by the rules capping the amount of political donations. Tobacco gave some $6.8 million of its total contributions in this form.
Philip Morris, maker of the popular Marlboro brand, donated nearly $3 million to the Republican and Democratic parties in 1995-96, making it by far the nation's top contributor of soft money.
R.J. Reynolds, maker of the Camel brand, was third in soft money, handing out $1.4 million in 1995-96.
